html:
Samye is the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet, built in the Yarlung Tsangpo valley southeast of Lhasa under King Trisong Detsen of the Tibetan Empire. Sources date its building variously between about 763 and 779; the first Tibetan monks were ordained there in 779.

The Indian abbot Shantarakshita planned it, and tradition says the tantric master Padmasambhava tamed the local spirits who kept knocking down the walls. Its layout is a mandala, a model of the Buddhist universe: a central temple stands for Mount Meru, with smaller temples around it for the continents, the sun and the moon, all inside a round wall.

Here, around 792 to 794, the king held the Samye debate, which set Indian teaching of gradual awakening against Chinese Chan (Zen). The Indian side was declared the winner, and Tibet followed Indian Buddhism from then on (see Buddhism made the state religion). Samye belongs to the Nyingma school. It was wrecked in the Cultural Revolution and rebuilt from the 1980s.
